gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 140 W these banks advertise exists only as the 28 V × 5 A level USB PD 3.1 added, so it needs a 240 W-rated cable and a laptop that takes 28 V, and on the UGREEN 145W it falls to 100 W once a second device is plugged in.
standout_why: Compared against Dupple (cited), both Powerbanks.fyi pages (one cited) and the Android Central review. Dupple only says of the UGREEN 145W that 'A 0.5 m 240 W USB-C cable is included' at $79.99, and does not mention PD version, PPS or multi-port power drop. Powerbanks.fyi says nothing about cables, PD version or port splits for any 25,000 mAh bank. ChatGPT's own answer says the UGREEN needs 'separate charging cables' without saying which rating. None gives the 28 V rule or the 100 W + 45 W split. TechRadar's body, Best Buy, the INIU collection and the UGREEN collection page could not be read (truncated, timeout, HTTP 429), so standout is judged without them.
decides: It confirms the UGREEN 145W as the under-$100 pick for a 16-inch MacBook Pro or other 140 W laptop, with conditions: use a 240 W cable (UGREEN US lists one at $13.99, or the bank + 240 W cable bundle at $75.98, both under $100) and charge the laptop alone on USB-C1. For laptops that fast-charge at 96 W or less (Apple lists 96 W for the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 70 W for MacBook Air), the 140 W port adds nothing over a 100 W bank, so weight, built-in cables or price should decide. Samsung owners should note Android Central found no 25 W / 45 W PPS charging on its 2023 unit, though UGREEN's sheet lists PPS.

findings.label: Why 140 W needs PD 3.1 (USB-IF's words)
findings.value: "New 28V, 36V, and 48V fixed voltages enable up to 140W, 180W and 240W power levels, respectively." Before that, "USB PD was limited to 100W using a solution based on 20V using USB Type-C cables rated at 5A."
findings.note: Arithmetic: 20 V × 5 A = 100 W; 28 V × 5 A = 140 W. Current stays at 5 A, so the extra 40 W comes only from the 28 V level.

findings.label: Cable requirement above 100 W (USB-IF's words)
findings.value: "The USB Type-C specification has also been updated to Release 2.1 to define 240W cable requirements"; the page describes "delivering up to 240W of power over full featured USB Type-C cable and connector."
findings.note: This page does not spell out that a 100 W cable caps a 140 W port at 100 W; that sentence was not sourced (see unsourced).
